before.title: Calculus of separated phasor fields: real-part derivative identities and amplitude injectivity
before.reference: core-conditional-proofs.md#K9; scaffold-added necessary prerequisite (see batch-35 notes)
before.strategy: Differentiate each component of $\operatorname{Re}(we^{i\theta})$ with $w=\tilde F_j$ by the product and chain rules for real and imaginary parts ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]), using $\operatorname{Re}(i\zeta)=-\operatorname{Im}\zeta$ and $\operatorname{Re}(-i\zeta)=\operatorname{Im}\zeta$; assemble the divergence and curl componentwise. For (d), write $C=a+ib$ with real $a,b$; the two scalar equations $a\cos\varphi_j-b\sin\varphi_j=0$ ($j=1,2$) form a real $2\times2$ system of determinant $\sin(\varphi_1-\varphi_2)$ for each component, hence $a_j=b_j=0$. If $F=G$ on an open $U$, then for every $x_t$ in the projection the phases attained in the open fibres include two values whose difference is not in $\pi\mathbb Z$ (an open fibre contains points with any phase in an interval of positive length), so $\tilde F(x_t)=\tilde G(x_t)$. The projection of a nonempty open set is nonempty and open.

before.reference: completed-expansion-arguments.md#G1-G2; scaffold-added necessary prerequisite (see batch-35 notes)

before.title: The sine and cosine systems are complete orthogonal systems of L^2 on an interval and on a rectangle
before.reference: completed-expansion-arguments.md#G2; scaffold-added necessary prerequisite (see batch-35 notes)
before.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $L>0$ and $R=(0,L_1)\times(0,L_2)$ with $L_1,L_2>0$.
(a) [One interval] The families $\{\cos(m\pi x/L)\}_{m\ge0}$ and $\{\sin(m\pi x/L)\}_{m\ge1}$ are orthogonal complete systems in the real Hilbert space $L^2(0,L)$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]], [[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]): each is orthogonal, and its closed linear span is all of $L^2(0,L)$.
(b) [Rectangle] With $m,n$ ranging over $\mathbb N_0$ in cosine slots and over $\mathbb N_{\ge1}$ in sine slots, each of the four product families $\{\cos\frac{m\pi x_1}{L_1}\cos\frac{n\pi x_2}{L_2}\}$, $\{\cos\frac{m\pi x_1}{L_1}\sin\frac{n\pi x_2}{L_2}\}$, $\{\sin\frac{m\pi x_1}{L_1}\cos\frac{n\pi x_2}{L_2}\}$ and $\{\sin\frac{m\pi x_1}{L_1}\sin\frac{n\pi x_2}{L_2}\}$ is an orthogonal complete system in $L^2(R)$; in particular the Neumann family $\{h_{mn}\}_{m,n\ge0}$ and the Dirichlet family $\{e_{mn}\}_{m,n\ge1}$ of [[lem-em-rectangle-mode-profile-identities]] are orthogonal complete systems in $L^2(R)$.
before.strategy: (a) Rescale $x=L u/\pi$ to period $2\pi$ ([[thm-linear-change-of-variables-for-lebesgue-measure]]). For $f\in L^2(0,L)$ orthogonal to every $\cos(m\pi x/L)$, extend $f$ evenly to $(-L,L)$ and $2L$-periodically; the extended $F$ lies in $L^2$ of the torus and every character coefficient $\widehat F(k)$ is a fixed multiple of $\int_0^Lf(x)\cos(k\pi x/L)\,dx$, computed by splitting the integral at $0$ and substituting $x\mapsto-x$ on $(-L,0)$ ([[cor-c-one-change-of-variables-for-l-one-functions]]); hence all coefficients vanish and [[thm-trigonometric-system-is-complete-in-l-two-of-the-torus]] gives $F=0$, so $f=0$. The sine case uses the odd extension, whose character coefficients are the sine coefficients (the $k=0$ coefficient vanishes identically). (b) Orthogonality is product integration. If $f\in L^2(R)$ is orthogonal to every $c_m(x_1)d_n(x_2)$, then for each $m$ the function $g_m(x_2):=\int_0^{L_1}f(x_1,x_2)c_m(x_1)\,dx_1$ is in $L^2(0,L_2)$ by Cauchy-Schwarz and Fubini ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]], [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]), and $\int_0^{L_2}g_md_n=0$ for all $n$ by Fubini, so $g_m=0$ a.e. by (a). Taking the countable union of the exceptional null sets, for a.e. $x_2$ one has $\int_0^{L_1}f(x_1,x_2)c_m(x_1)\,dx_1=0$ for all $m$, so $f(\cdot,x_2)=0$ a.e. in $x_1$ by (a), and Fubini gives $f=0$ a.e. Completeness as closed span is therefore established; the orthogonal expansions converge in $L^2$ by [[thm-hilbert-space-fourier-expansion]]. The argument is symmetric in the four parity choices.

before.title: Rectangular PEC guide and cavity geometry, the zero-normal-B reflection class, and axis-relative TE/TM/TEM
before.statement:
Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, its SI units and its fields $E,B$ be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-si-conventions]] and [[def-em-fields]]. Fix $a,b>0$, write $x_t=(x_1,x_2)$, $e_z:=e_3$, and let $\nabla_t,\Delta_t,\operatorname{div}_t$ be the transverse gradient, Laplacian and divergence.
(a) [Straight guide] A straight guide region is $\Omega_A:=A\times\mathbb R$ for a bounded connected $C^1$ plane domain $A\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ ([[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]), with longitudinal axis $e_z$; for a rectangular cross-section $A=R_{ab}:=(0,a)\times(0,b)$ the region is called the rectangular guide and its walls are the four open faces $\{x_1=0\},\{x_1=a\},\{x_2=0\},\{x_2=b\}$. A rectangular cavity region is $\Omega_c:=(0,a)\times(0,b)\times(0,d)$ for fixed $d>0$, with the six open faces as its walls. Spatial derivatives are taken at fixed $t$; the fields are defined on $\Omega\times I$ with the regularity declared by each theorem.
(b) [PEC boundary model] On every open wall (a wall minus its edges) the ideal perfectly conducting boundary model declares the two conditions $n\times E=0$ and $n\cdot B=0$, where $n$ is the outward unit normal of that wall ($-e_1,+e_1,-e_2,+e_2$ on the four rectangular walls, and $\pm e_j$ on the six cavity walls). Its physical reading is the ideal-conductor limit of the stationary interface conditions of [[pthm-em-material-stationary-jumps]]: with $E=B=0$ inside the ideal conductor the tangential electric field and the normal magnetic field vanish, while the surface-charge and surface-current readings $n\cdot D=\sigma_f$ and $n\times H=K_f$ are determined by the traces and are not prescribed here. The supplier's hypotheses (a compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface with one-sided $C^1$ fields) cover a smooth stationary interface, not the $\sigma\to\infty$ idealization nor the box edges; the guide/cavity conditions on the open walls are therefore declared as an idealization of this definition, and no pointwise statement on the edges is made.
(c) [Zero-normal-B reflection class] For the rectangular box $Q=\prod_{j=1}^3(0,L_j)$ with $L=(a,b,d)$, the reflection class is the class of locally integrable fields $E,B$ on $Q$ whose extensions to the rectangular torus $\prod_j\mathbb R/(2L_j\mathbb Z)$, defined by extending $E_1$ evenly across the $x_1$-walls and oddly across the $x_2$-, $x_3$-walls and cyclically for $E_2,E_3$, and extending $B_1$ oddly across $x_1$ and evenly across $x_2,x_3$ and cyclically for $B_2,B_3$, are $L^2$ fields, together with the distributional constraints that $\operatorname{div}E$ and $\operatorname{div}B$ vanish on the torus for the extensions. This is the declared weak PEC model used for the cavity initial-value problem; for smooth fields the parities give $n\times E=0$ and $n\cdot B=0$ on $\partial Q$. Initial data not in this class (for example data with trapped normal $B$) are excluded, as are the general $H(\operatorname{curl})$ boundary classes, which are defined by the mathematical suppliers and are not identified here with the classical conditions.
(d) [TE, TM, TEM] For a guide or cavity field $(E,B)$, the longitudinal components are $E_z:=E\cdot e_z$ and $B_z:=B\cdot e_z$; the field is called TE (transverse electric) if $E_z\equiv0$, TM (transverse magnetic) if $B_z\equiv0$, and TEM if both vanish, always relative to the named axis $e_z$.
(e) [Separated phasor convention] For $\omega>0$ and $\beta\in\mathbb R$, a $\beta$-$\omega$ separated phasor field on the guide is a real field of the form $F(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\tilde F(x_1,x_2)e^{i(\beta x_3-\omega t)}\bigr)$ with a complex amplitude $\tilde F$, componentwise; $\omega/(2\pi)$ is the frequency and $\beta$ the longitudinal wave number, with $\beta>0$ describing propagation in the $+e_z$ direction under this phase convention.
(f) [Scope] The definition fixes the geometry, the PEC boundary model, the weak reflection class and the mode terminology; it asserts no field equation, no constitutive law and no existence or completeness of modes, and circular, non-rectangular, open-ended, junction and lossy guides or cavities are outside it.
before.strategy: An explicit type/domain/convention definition: geometry and transversality are fixed by coordinates and normals; the PEC model is declared with its interface reading and its excluded idealization/edges; the reflection class is defined by the reflection rules and distributional divergence constraints; the phasor convention is stated as an encoding of real fields. No differential equation is introduced.
before.physical_scope: The ideal PEC boundary model of the straight rectangular guide and cavity (and of straight guides with a bounded connected C1 cross-section) in the lossless laboratory chart, together with the zero-normal-B reflection class and the TE/TM/TEM classification. The boundary model is an idealization of an interface with a perfectly conducting medium on the open walls; the definition asserts no field equations, constitutive laws or mode completeness.

after.title: Rectangular PEC guide and cavity geometry, the zero-normal-B reflection class, and axis-relative TE/TM/TEM
after.statement:
Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, its SI units and its fields $E,B$ be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-si-conventions]] and [[def-em-fields]]. Fix $a,b>0$, write $x_t=(x_1,x_2)$, $e_z:=e_3$, and define $\nabla_t f=(\partial_1f,\partial_2f,0)$, $\Delta_t f=\partial_1^2f+\partial_2^2f$ and $\operatorname{div}_tu_t=\partial_1u_1+\partial_2u_2$ for the stated regularity, using [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]].
(a) [Straight guide] A straight guide region is $\Omega_A:=A\times\mathbb R$ where $A$ is either a bounded connected $C^1$ plane domain ([[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]) or the explicit rectangular cross-section; the rectangle has corners and is treated by its open faces, not asserted to be a $C^1$ boundary domain, with longitudinal axis $e_z$; for a rectangular cross-section $A=R_{ab}:=(0,a)\times(0,b)$ the region is called the rectangular guide and its walls are the four open faces $\{x_1=0\},\{x_1=a\},\{x_2=0\},\{x_2=b\}$. A rectangular cavity region is $\Omega_c:=(0,a)\times(0,b)\times(0,d)$ for fixed $d>0$, with the six open faces as its walls. The separate smooth-cavity spectral branch uses an explicitly declared bounded $C^\infty$ domain in $\mathbb R^3$ with its smooth PEC boundary; it is not the rectangular reflection class. Spatial derivatives are taken at fixed $t$; the fields are defined on $\Omega\times I$ with the regularity declared by each theorem.
(b) [PEC boundary model] On every open wall (a wall minus its edges) the ideal perfectly conducting boundary model declares the two conditions $n\times E=0$ and $n\cdot B=0$, where $n$ is the outward unit normal of that wall ($-e_1,+e_1,-e_2,+e_2$ on the four rectangular walls, and $\pm e_j$ on the six cavity walls). Its physical reading is the ideal-conductor limit of the stationary interface conditions of [[pthm-em-material-stationary-jumps]]: with $E=B=0$ inside the ideal conductor the tangential electric field and the normal magnetic field vanish, while the surface-charge and surface-current readings $n\cdot D=\sigma_f$ and $n\times H=K_f$ are determined by the traces and are not prescribed here. The supplier's hypotheses (a compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface with one-sided $C^1$ fields) cover a smooth stationary interface, not the $\sigma\to\infty$ idealization nor the box edges; the guide/cavity conditions on the open walls are therefore declared as an idealization of this definition, and no pointwise statement on the edges is made.
(c) [Zero-normal-B reflection class] For the rectangular box $Q=\prod_{j=1}^3(0,L_j)$ with $L=(a,b,d)$, the reflection class is the class of locally integrable fields $E,B$ on $Q$ whose extensions to the rectangular torus $\prod_j\mathbb R/(2L_j\mathbb Z)$, defined by extending $E_1$ evenly across the $x_1$-walls and oddly across the $x_2$-, $x_3$-walls and cyclically for $E_2,E_3$, and extending $B_1$ oddly across $x_1$ and evenly across $x_2,x_3$ and cyclically for $B_2,B_3$, are $L^2$ fields, together with the distributional constraints that $\operatorname{div}E$ and $\operatorname{div}B$ vanish on the torus for the extensions. This is the declared weak PEC model used for the cavity initial-value problem; for smooth fields the parities give $n\times E=0$ and $n\cdot B=0$ on $\partial Q$. Initial data not in this class (for example data with trapped normal $B$) are excluded, as are the general $H(\operatorname{curl})$ boundary classes, which are defined by the mathematical suppliers and are not identified here with the classical conditions.
(d) [TE, TM, TEM] For a guide or cavity field $(E,B)$, the longitudinal components are $E_z:=E\cdot e_z$ and $B_z:=B\cdot e_z$; the field is called TE (transverse electric) if $E_z\equiv0$, TM (transverse magnetic) if $B_z\equiv0$, and TEM if both vanish, always relative to the named axis $e_z$.
(e) [Separated phasor convention] For $\omega>0$ and $\beta\in\mathbb C$, a $\beta$-$\omega$ separated phasor field on the guide is a real field of the form $F(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\tilde F(x_1,x_2)e^{i(\beta x_3-\omega t)}\bigr)$ with a complex amplitude $\tilde F$, componentwise; $\omega/(2\pi)$ is the frequency and $\beta$ the longitudinal propagation constant; when $\beta$ is real, $\beta>0$ describes propagation in the $+e_z$ direction under this phase convention, while a complex $\beta$ gives the spatial factor $e^{-\operatorname{Im}\beta x_3}$ and may grow in the opposite direction; each consuming branch states its selection.
(f) [Scope] The definition fixes the geometry, the PEC boundary model, the weak reflection class and the mode terminology; it asserts no field equation, no constitutive law and no existence or completeness of modes, Rectangular TE/TM candidates and the rectangular reflection class, declared smooth bounded PEC cavity spectral classes, and smooth straight-guide TEM potential branches (including the coaxial annulus) are within this geometry. No general non-rectangular TE/TM guide theory, circular-guide spectral classification, open-end or junction scattering, or lossy model is supplied.
after.strategy: An explicit type/domain/convention definition: geometry and transversality are fixed by coordinates and normals; the PEC model is declared with its interface reading and its excluded idealization/edges; the reflection class is defined by the reflection rules and distributional divergence constraints; the phasor convention is stated as an encoding of real fields. No differential equation is introduced.
after.physical_scope: The ideal PEC boundary model of the straight rectangular guide and cavity (and of straight guides with a bounded connected C1 cross-section) in the lossless laboratory chart, together with the zero-normal-B reflection class and the TE/TM/TEM classification. The boundary model is an idealization of an interface with a perfectly conducting medium on the open walls; the definition asserts no field equations, constitutive laws or mode completeness.

before.title: Complete mode expansions of the declared guide and cavity classes: transverse profile completeness, the rectangular reflection class and the smooth PEC cavity eigenbasis
before.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice as declared by the cited mathematical suppliers ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]), the lossless isotropic scalar constant branch of [[post-em-material-closure]] with $\varepsilon,\mu>0$ and $\sigma=0$, the macroscopic equations of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]] with $\rho_f=0$, $J_f=0$, and the guide, cavity, PEC and reflection-class conventions of [[def-em-guide-cavity-geometry]].
(a) [Transverse profile completeness] For the cross-section $(0,a)\times(0,b)$, the families $\{h_{mn}\}_{m,n\ge0}$ and $\{e_{mn}\}_{m,n\ge1}$ of [[lem-em-rectangle-mode-profile-identities]] are orthogonal complete systems in $L^2$ of the rectangle ([[lem-em-rectangular-transverse-mode-completeness]]); hence the transverse scalar profiles of the TE and TM candidates of [[pthm-em-rectangular-mode-candidates]] exhaust the transverse $L^2$ profiles, with the orthogonal expansions converging in $L^2$.
(b) [Rectangular cavity reflection class] For the box $Q=(0,a)\times(0,b)\times(0,d)$ with the reflection class and distributional constraints $\operatorname{div}E=\operatorname{div}B=0$ of [[def-em-guide-cavity-geometry]](c): the finite separated Fourier modes are dense in the class at every time; every initial datum in the class has a unique $C(\mathbb R;L^2)$ weak solution of the lossless first-order system $\partial_tE=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1}\operatorname{curl}B$, $\partial_tB=-\operatorname{curl}E$ in the same class, with derivatives as in [[def-distributional-derivative]]; along the solution the total stored energy $\int_Q u\,dx$ equals $\frac12\int_Q(\varepsilon|E|^2+|B|^2/\mu)\,dx$ and is constant, where $u$ is the stored-energy density of [[pthm-em-restricted-material-energy]]. For $C^1$-in-time solutions the four macroscopic equations with $D=\varepsilon E$, $B=\mu H$ hold distributionally.
(c) [Smooth PEC cavity] For a bounded $C^\infty$ cavity domain $\Omega$ and the PEC class $X,V,H$ of [[thm-em-waveguide-spectral-completeness]](a): the curl form on $V$ has a complete orthonormal $L^2$ eigenbasis $\{u_j\}$ with nonnegative eigenvalues $\lambda_j$ of finite multiplicity, $\lambda_j\to\infty$ whenever $H$ is infinite dimensional, and a finite-dimensional zero eigenspace that is retained; the eigen-equation $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}u_j=\lambda_ju_j$ holds distributionally with the PEC trace, and each $u_j$ has a $C^\infty$ representative on the closure. For the first-order lossless system in this class the coefficients $a_j(t):=\langle E(\cdot,t),u_j\rangle$ of a smooth-in-time solution satisfy $a_j''+(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1}\lambda_ja_j=0$, the finitely many $\lambda_j=0$ coefficients are affine in $t$, and the finite-energy expansions converge in $C_tV\cap C_tH$ as in the cited supplier for the associated second-order wave.
(d) [Scope] The theorem asserts completeness only for the transverse $L^2$ profiles and for the two declared cavity classes with their exact hypotheses; it asserts no completeness for the unbounded guide's longitudinal expansion, and none for lossy, dispersive, open-ended, non-smooth, non-rectangular or exterior problems, no trace regularity for arbitrary $H(\operatorname{curl})$ fields, and no identification of the weak classes with every maximal tangential-trace realization. The zero eigenvalues and zero modes are retained throughout.

after.title: Complete mode expansions of the declared guide and cavity classes: transverse profile completeness, the rectangular reflection class and the smooth PEC cavity eigenbasis
after.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice as declared by the cited mathematical suppliers ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]), the lossless isotropic scalar constant branch of [[post-em-material-closure]] with $\varepsilon,\mu>0$ and $\sigma=0$, the source-free smooth macroscopic equations of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]] in the smooth branches, with $\rho_f=0$, $J_f=0$, and the explicitly declared weak first-order material equations in the weak cavity branches below, and the guide, cavity, PEC and reflection-class conventions of [[def-em-guide-cavity-geometry]].
(a) [Transverse profile completeness] For the cross-section $(0,a)\times(0,b)$, the families $\{h_{mn}\}_{m,n\ge0}$ and $\{e_{mn}\}_{m,n\ge1}$ of [[lem-em-rectangle-mode-profile-identities]] are orthogonal complete systems in $L^2$ of the rectangle ([[lem-em-rectangular-transverse-mode-completeness]]); The full scalar Neumann and Dirichlet families have these $L^2$ expansions. The physical TE candidate family excludes $h_{00}=1$ by the full Maxwell equations: the remaining $h_{mn}$ are complete in the zero-mean subspace $\{f\in L^2:\int_Rf=0\}$, not in all scalar $L^2$. The Dirichlet TM profiles retain their full scalar completeness. The constant Neumann scalar profile is retained in the mathematical basis but is not asserted to be a nonzero positive-frequency TE mode.
(b) [Rectangular cavity reflection class] For the box $Q=(0,a)\times(0,b)\times(0,d)$ with the reflection class and distributional constraints $\operatorname{div}E=\operatorname{div}B=0$ of [[def-em-guide-cavity-geometry]](c): the finite separated Fourier modes are dense in the class at every time; every initial datum in the class has a unique $C(\mathbb R;L^2)$ weak solution of the lossless first-order system $\partial_tE=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1}\operatorname{curl}B$, $\partial_tB=-\operatorname{curl}E$ in the same class, with derivatives as in [[def-distributional-derivative]]; this lossless first-order distributional system is the explicitly adopted weak material evolution of the reflection model, not inferred from the smooth-only hypotheses of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]]; along the solution the total stored energy $\int_Q u\,dx$ equals $\frac12\int_Q(\varepsilon|E|^2+|B|^2/\mu)\,dx$ and is constant, where the weak stored-energy density is defined almost everywhere by this nonnegative quadratic expression, consistent with the smooth local definition of [[pthm-em-restricted-material-energy]]. Its integrability and constancy are furnished by the mathematical reflection-class energy result; no nonlinear weak Poynting identity is asserted. For $C^1$-in-time solutions the four macroscopic equations with $D=\varepsilon E$, $B=\mu H$ hold distributionally.
(c) [Smooth PEC cavity] For a bounded $C^\infty$ cavity domain $\Omega$ and the PEC class $X,V,H$ of [[thm-em-waveguide-spectral-completeness]](a): the curl form on $V$ has a complete orthonormal $L^2$ eigenbasis $\{u_j\}$ with nonnegative eigenvalues $\lambda_j$ of finite multiplicity, $\lambda_j\to\infty$ whenever $H$ is infinite dimensional, and a finite-dimensional zero eigenspace that is retained; the eigen-equation $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}u_j=\lambda_ju_j$ holds distributionally with the PEC trace, and each $u_j$ has a $C^\infty$ representative on the closure. Put $v_{\mathrm{wave}}=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1/2}>0$. The associated second-order electric wave has the full supplied interface: for arbitrary initial displacement in $V$ and velocity in $H$, its displacement is in $C(\mathbb R;V)$, its velocity in $C(\mathbb R;H)$, and finite modal sums converge in these respective norms uniformly on compact time intervals. Its zero eigenmodes may be affine in time. Separately, let $J$ be an open time interval and let a strong first-order solution obey $E\in C^1(J;H)\cap C(J;V)$ and $B\in C^1(J;L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3))\cap C(J;H(\operatorname{curl}))$, with the first-order equations as $L^2$ identities and both distributional divergence constraints. Electric tangential-zero boundary data are encoded by $E(t)\in V$. The magnetic normal-zero condition is declared weakly by $\int_\Omega B(t)\cdot\nabla\psi=0$ for every smooth scalar $\psi$ on the closure; when $B\in C^1(\overline\Omega)$ this is $n\cdot B=0$, using $\operatorname{div}B=0$. No magnetic membership in the electric tangential-zero class $X$ is assumed. Then $a_j(t):=\langle E(t),u_j\rangle$ is $C^2$ and satisfies $a_j''+v_{\mathrm{wave}}^2\lambda_ja_j=0$. For $\lambda_j=0$, the admissible first-order coefficients satisfy $a_j'=0$ and are constant, with the zero eigenfields retained. This extra compatibility distinguishes first-order Maxwell data from arbitrary second-order $V\times H$ data; it does not remove the broader supplied second-order wave or its affine zero modes.
(d) [Scope] The theorem asserts completeness only for the transverse $L^2$ profiles and for the two declared cavity classes with their exact hypotheses; it asserts no completeness for the unbounded guide's longitudinal expansion, and none for lossy, dispersive, open-ended, non-smooth or exterior problems, or arbitrary non-rectangular guide problems beyond the explicitly declared smooth-cavity spectral class, no trace regularity for arbitrary $H(\operatorname{curl})$ fields, and no identification of the weak classes with every maximal tangential-trace realization. The zero eigenvalues and zero modes are retained throughout.
after.strategy: Clause (a) is [[lem-em-rectangular-transverse-mode-completeness]](b) instantiated at the cross-section, whose profiles are those of the candidate theorem. Clause (b) is the rectangular reflection-class lemma [[lem-em-rectangular-pec-energy-completeness]] read physically, as packaged in [[thm-em-waveguide-spectral-completeness]](b): the class, the first-order system, density of finite separated modes, unique $C_tL^2$ weak solutions and constant energy all come from that supplier; the identification of the energy with $\int_Qu$ uses $D=\varepsilon E$, $B=\mu H$ and [[pthm-em-restricted-material-energy]](a), and the macroscopic equations follow from the two evolution equations together with the distributional divergence constraints of the class. For the scalar basis distinction in (a), every nonconstant Neumann product is orthogonal to $h_{00}=1$, and the complete orthogonal expansion of [[lem-em-rectangular-transverse-mode-completeness]] shows that deleting that one basis element gives precisely its orthogonal complement, the zero-mean subspace. The constant scalar element remains in the full basis and is excluded only as a monochromatic TE reconstruction. In (b), the explicit weak first-order model is solved by [[lem-em-rectangular-pec-energy-completeness]] as packaged in the wrapper; its Fourier energy proof gives the quadratic energy conservation without applying a smooth-only local balance to rough fields. For (c), [[thm-em-waveguide-spectral-completeness]] supplies the spectral and smooth-eigenfield assertions and the associated wave at the positive parameter $v_{\mathrm{wave}}=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1/2}$, with its exact arbitrary $V\times H$ initial-data interface, displacement $C_tV$ and velocity $C_tH$. To derive the first-order coefficient equations, prove the actual curl pairing against each smooth PEC eigenfield $u_j$, not an unproved equality of electric and magnetic boundary classes. A smooth normal collar of the compact boundary exists by [[thm-euclidean-tubular-neighbourhood-theorem]]. Write $s$ for the inward normal coordinate (its gradient is the negative extended unit normal) and use the standard smooth step [[def-the-standard-smooth-step-function]] to set a cutoff $\eta_\delta=0$ for $s\le\delta$ and $1$ for $s\ge2\delta$. The normal tube has bounded Jacobians on the compact collar. Since $n\times u_j=0$ on the boundary and $u_j$ is smooth, $|n\times u_j|\le Cs$ in the collar. Thus $\eta_\delta u_j\to u_j$ and $\operatorname{curl}(\eta_\delta u_j)\to\operatorname{curl}u_j$ in $L^2$: the derivative-cutoff term is bounded on a layer of volume $O(\delta)$ because $|\nabla\eta_\delta|\le C/\delta$ and its cross product with $u_j$ is $O(s/\delta)$. For every $F\in H(\operatorname{curl})$, the distributional identity on the compactly supported smooth test $\eta_\delta u_j$ is $\langle\operatorname{curl}F,\eta_\delta u_j\rangle=\langle F,\operatorname{curl}(\eta_\delta u_j)\rangle$. Cauchy-Schwarz and the two $L^2$ limits give $\langle\operatorname{curl}F,u_j\rangle=\langle F,\operatorname{curl}u_j\rangle$. Apply this only to $F=B(t)$, which has the stated actual graph regularity. Then $a_j'=v_{\mathrm{wave}}^2\langle B,\operatorname{curl}u_j\rangle$. The assumed $B\in C^1_tL^2$ permits one further scalar derivative, giving $a_j''=v_{\mathrm{wave}}^2\langle B',\operatorname{curl}u_j\rangle=-v_{\mathrm{wave}}^2\langle\operatorname{curl}E,\operatorname{curl}u_j\rangle=-v_{\mathrm{wave}}^2\lambda_j\langle E,u_j\rangle$ by the full-$X$ eigenvariational identity of [[lem-em-smooth-pec-cavity-spectral-closure]], since $E(t)\in V\subset X$. No second time derivative of the whole field is assumed. If $\lambda_j=0$, that identity tested at $u_j$ gives $\operatorname{curl}u_j=0$, so the preceding formula for $a_j'$ is zero. Such electric zero modes are constant under first-order Maxwell evolution, while the associated unrestricted second-order equation retains affine zero modes. Divergence constraints and the declared magnetic normal condition remain part of the physical model; the pairing does not impose a magnetic electric-type trace. The inherited AC and AComega assumptions cover the spectral/Fourier and collar suppliers. No lossy or open-domain step is made.
after.physical_scope: The completeness statements available for the declared classes of the lossless isotropic scalar constant branch: transverse L^2 profile completeness of the TE/TM families on the rectangular cross-section, the rectangular cavity reflection class with its unique finite-energy weak solutions and constant stored energy, and the smooth bounded PEC cavity curl eigenbasis with modal expansions retaining zero modes. before.title: The TE10 candidate of an empty rectangular guide: explicit fields, cutoff and propagating branch
before.statement: Let $\varepsilon,\mu>0$, $a,b>0$, $\omega>0$, $\beta>0$ with $\beta^2=\omega^2\varepsilon\mu-(\pi/a)^2>0$, and put $\omega_c:=\pi/(a\sqrt{\varepsilon\mu})$, $\theta:=\beta x_3-\omega t$. In the rectangular guide of [[def-em-guide-cavity-geometry]] with cross-section $(0,a)\times(0,b)$, take the TE candidate of [[pthm-em-rectangular-mode-candidates]](a) with $(m,n)=(1,0)$, whose amplitudes are $$\tilde E=\bigl(0,\,i\omega\mu\tfrac{a}{\pi}\sin\tfrac{\pi x_1}{a},\,0\bigr),\qquad \tilde H=\bigl(-i\beta\tfrac{a}{\pi}\sin\tfrac{\pi x_1}{a},\,0,\,\cos\tfrac{\pi x_1}{a}\bigr).$$ Then the real fields $E=\operatorname{Re}(\tilde Ee^{i\theta})$, $B=\mu\operatorname{Re}(\tilde He^{i\theta})$ are smooth, have $E_z=0$ (TE) with $E$ linearly polarized along $e_2$, satisfy the source-free lossless macroscopic equations and the PEC wall conditions, and carry a half-sine standing profile $\sin(\pi x_1/a)$ in $x_1$ with a traveling wave in $x_3$. The cutoff of this mode is $\omega_c=\pi/(a\sqrt{\varepsilon\mu})$: real nonzero $\beta$ exists exactly for $\omega>\omega_c$, at $\omega=\omega_c$ the mode is at cutoff ($\beta=0$), and for $\omega<\omega_c$ it is evanescent. If $a\ge b$, then $\omega_c=\pi/(a\sqrt{\varepsilon\mu})$ is the lowest cutoff of all TE indices and of all modes (attained also by $(m,n)=(0,1)$ when $a=b$); the case $(m,n)=(0,0)$ is not a mode by the index restriction of the theorem. This is an explicit conditional candidate of the adopted model; it asserts no measurement and no completeness.

before.title: TEM modes of a coaxial guide and the single-conductor obstruction for harmonic transverse potentials
before.statement:
Assume the lossless isotropic scalar constant branch of [[post-em-material-closure]], the macroscopic equations of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]] with $\rho_f=0$, $J_f=0$, and the straight-guide, TEM and separated-phasor conventions of [[def-em-guide-cavity-geometry]]; put $Z:=\sqrt{\mu/\varepsilon}$ and $v:=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1/2}$.
(a) [Potential form] Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be a bounded connected $C^1$ domain and let $\varphi\in C^2(\overline A;\mathbb R)$ satisfy $\Delta\varphi=0$ on $A$ (the plane Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]; a $C^2$ function with $\Delta\varphi=0$ is called harmonic). Define $\tilde E:=-\nabla\varphi$, $k:=\omega/v$ and $\tilde H:=\frac1Ze_z\times\tilde E$; then the separated real fields $E=\operatorname{Re}(\tilde Ee^{i(kx_3-\omega t)})$, $B=\mu\operatorname{Re}(\tilde He^{i(kx_3-\omega t)})$ satisfy the source-free lossless macroscopic equations with $E_z=B_z=0$ (TEM), and the PEC condition on a smooth wall with unit normal $n$ is equivalent to $\partial_\tau\varphi=0$ along that boundary curve, so that $\varphi$ is constant on each connected component of $\partial A$. Moreover, if $A$ is star-shaped ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]), every separated TEM phasor field on the guide is of this potential form: its transverse electric amplitude is closed and divergence-free, hence exact by [[cor-closed-exact-and-conservative-equivalence-on-star-shaped-domains]] applied to its real and imaginary parts separately, and the equations force $\tilde H=\frac1Ze_z\times\tilde E$ and $k=\omega/v$.
(b) [Single-conductor obstruction] If in the potential-form setting $\partial A$ is connected, then $\varphi$ is constant on $\partial A$, hence $\varphi$ is constant on $\overline A$ by the two-dimensional classical Dirichlet uniqueness of [[cor-classical-dirichlet-and-poisson-problems-are-unique]] (with the constant as the second solution), and therefore $\tilde E=\tilde H=0$: a single-conductor cross-section with connected boundary admits no nonzero TEM field in the potential form. In particular the rectangular guide of [[def-em-guide-cavity-geometry]] (star-shaped, connected boundary) has no nonzero TEM candidate.
(c) [Coaxial example] Let $a<b$, $A:=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:a<|x|<b\}$ (two boundary components), fix $V\in\mathbb R$ and define $\varphi(x):=V\ln(b/|x|)/\ln(b/a)$, so that $\tilde E=V e_r/(|x|\ln(b/a))$ with $e_r:=x/|x|$ and $\tilde H=(V/(Z|x|\ln(b/a)))e_\varphi$ with $e_\varphi:=e_z\times e_r$. Then $\Delta\varphi=0$ on $A$: indeed $\partial_i\ln|x|=x_i/|x|^2$ by [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]] and the chain rule ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]), and the second partial derivatives sum to zero; hence $\varphi$ is constant on each boundary circle (values $V$ at $|x|=a$ and $0$ at $|x|=b$), the fields satisfy the source-free lossless macroscopic equations and the PEC conditions, and the relation $k=\omega/v$ is nondispersive with no cutoff. The amplitude integrals computed in polar coordinates with [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]] (the Jacobian factor $r$ is read from that formula) are $$W_e:=\tfrac12\varepsilon\int_A|\tilde E|^2\,dA=\tfrac12CV^2,\qquad W_m:=\tfrac12\mu\int_A|\tilde H|^2\,dA=\tfrac12CV^2,\qquad C:=\frac{2\pi\varepsilon}{\ln(b/a)};$$ the instantaneous per-length energies are $\tfrac12CV^2\cos^2\theta$ and $\tfrac12LI^2\cos^2\theta$ with $\theta=kx_3-\omega t$; equivalently, with $L:=\mu\ln(b/a)/(2\pi)$ and the boundary-current amplitude $I:=2\pi V/(Z\ln(b/a))$ one has $W_m=\tfrac12LI^2$ and $LC=\varepsilon\mu$. The two boundary components carrying distinct constants are exactly what the single-conductor obstruction excludes.
(d) [Scope] The obstruction clause (b) is proved for the potential form (equivalently, by (a), for star-shaped cross-sections); the general reduction of an arbitrary TEM field to the potential form on a merely simply connected non-star-shaped cross-section is not asserted here. The coaxial clause is an explicit conditional computation in the declared model with no empirical content; no lossy, radiation or signal-speed claim is made.
before.strategy: Clause (a): with $\tilde E=-\nabla\varphi$ the transverse curl vanishes and $\operatorname{div}\tilde E=-\Delta\varphi=0$; [[lem-em-separated-phasor-calculus]] reduces the four real equations to $\operatorname{curl}\tilde E=i\omega\mu\tilde H$, $\operatorname{curl}\tilde H=-i\omega\varepsilon\tilde E$, and substitution of $\tilde H=\frac1Ze_z\times\tilde E$ with $k=\omega/v$ verifies both by [[lem-em-transverse-vector-identities]](a). The boundary equivalence uses $n\cdot(e_z\times\tilde E)=\partial_\tau\varphi$ for the boundary tangent $\tau:=e_z\times n$ and the fundamental theorem along each connected boundary curve. In the star-shaped case, closedness of $\tilde E$ (forced by $\operatorname{curl}\tilde E=i\omega\mu\tilde H$ with $\tilde H_z=0$) makes it exact, and the transverse equations force $\tilde H$ and $k$ as displayed. Clause (b): constant $\varphi$ on the single boundary component, then Dirichlet uniqueness applied to $\varphi$ and the constant. Clause (c): $\Delta\varphi=0$ by the displayed direct differentiation; the radial integrals $\int_A|\tilde E|^2=\int_A|Z\tilde H|^2=2\pi V^2/\ln(b/a)$ are evaluated in polar coordinates; the constant $\varphi$ on each circle and the radial/tangential decomposition give the PEC conditions. Only the choice-free local clauses of [[pthm-em-restricted-material-energy]] are used for the energy reading; no empirical premise is used.
before.physical_scope: The explicit coaxial TEM candidate of the lossless isotropic scalar branch with its per-length capacitance and inductance, and the obstruction showing that a single-conductor cross-section with connected boundary admits no nonzero TEM field in the harmonic-potential form. Includes the star-shaped reduction clause; no general simply connected reduction, lossy or empirical claim.

after.title: TEM modes of a coaxial guide and the single-conductor obstruction for harmonic transverse potentials
after.statement:
Assume the lossless isotropic scalar constant branch of [[post-em-material-closure]], the macroscopic equations of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]] with $\rho_f=0$, $J_f=0$, and the straight-guide, TEM and separated-phasor conventions of [[def-em-guide-cavity-geometry]]; put $Z:=\sqrt{\mu/\varepsilon}$ and $v:=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1/2}$.
(a) [Potential form] Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be a bounded connected $C^1$ domain and let $\varphi\in C^2(\overline A;\mathbb C)$ (with real-valued potentials included) satisfy $\Delta\varphi=0$ on $A$ (the plane Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]; a $C^2$ function with $\Delta\varphi=0$ is called harmonic). For either sign $\zeta\in\{+1,-1\}$ define $\tilde E:=-\nabla\varphi$, $\beta:=\zeta\omega/v$ and $\tilde H:=\zeta e_z\times\tilde E/Z$; then the separated real fields $E=\operatorname{Re}(\tilde Ee^{i(\beta x_3-\omega t)})$, $B=\mu\operatorname{Re}(\tilde He^{i(\beta x_3-\omega t)})$ satisfy the source-free lossless macroscopic equations with $E_z=B_z=0$ (TEM), and the PEC condition on a smooth wall with unit normal $n$ is equivalent to $\partial_\tau\varphi=0$ along that boundary curve, so that $\varphi$ is constant on each connected component of $\partial A$. Moreover, if $A$ is star-shaped ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]), every separated TEM phasor with $C^1$ transverse amplitudes has on the interior a complex harmonic potential $\varphi\in C^2(A;\mathbb C)$, obtained by applying [[cor-closed-exact-and-conservative-equivalence-on-star-shaped-domains]] to the real and imaginary electric amplitudes separately. If the field is nonzero, the equations force $\beta^2=\varepsilon\mu\omega^2$, hence $\beta=\pm\omega/v$, and $\tilde H=\beta e_z\times\tilde E/(\omega\mu)$, giving the two displayed signs. If the field is zero, $\tilde E=\tilde H=0$ solves the equations for every longitudinal label $\beta$, with no dispersion conclusion. The boundary potential description requires the stated continuous differentiable boundary trace (in particular the initial $C^2(\overline A)$ potential has it); the interior exactness supplier alone is not asserted to produce a real potential or automatic boundary extension.
(b) [Single-conductor obstruction] If in the potential-form setting $\partial A$ is connected, then $\varphi$ is constant on $\partial A$, hence $\varphi$ is constant on $\overline A$ by the two-dimensional classical Dirichlet uniqueness [[cor-uniqueness-for-the-classical-dirichlet-problem]], applied to its real and imaginary parts with their respective constants as second solutions, and therefore $\tilde E=\tilde H=0$: a single-conductor cross-section with connected boundary admits no nonzero TEM field in the potential form. The same potential-form obstruction applies to a rectangular cross-section with a potential in $C^2(A)\cap C(\overline A)$ having constant boundary trace, because this uniqueness supplier does not require a $C^1$ boundary. For rectangular separated TEM amplitudes that are $C^1$ on the interior and continuous on the closure with the classical PEC traces on open edges, the star-centre radial primitive extends continuously to the rectangle closure. The edgewise tangential derivative is the electric trace, so PEC makes the potential constant on each open edge and continuity joins those constants at the corners. Thus this stated rectangular class has no nonzero TEM field.
(c) [Coaxial example] For the following Lebesgue polar-coordinate energy calculation assume Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $0<a<b$, $A:=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:a<|x|<b\}$ (two boundary components), fix $V\in\mathbb R$, choose the forward label $k:=\omega/v$, and define $\varphi(x):=V\ln(b/|x|)/\ln(b/a)$, so that $\tilde E=V e_r/(|x|\ln(b/a))$ with $e_r:=x/|x|$ and $\tilde H=(V/(Z|x|\ln(b/a)))e_\varphi$ with $e_\varphi:=e_z\times e_r$. Then $\Delta\varphi=0$ on $A$: indeed $\partial_i\ln|x|=x_i/|x|^2$ by [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]] and the chain rule ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]), and the second partial derivatives sum to zero; hence $\varphi$ is constant on each boundary circle (values $V$ at $|x|=a$ and $0$ at $|x|=b$), the fields satisfy the source-free lossless macroscopic equations and the PEC conditions, and the relation $k=\omega/v$ is nondispersive with no cutoff. The amplitude integrals computed in polar coordinates with [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]] (the Jacobian factor $r$ is read from that formula) are $$W_e:=\tfrac12\varepsilon\int_A|\tilde E|^2\,dA=\tfrac12CV^2,\qquad W_m:=\tfrac12\mu\int_A|\tilde H|^2\,dA=\tfrac12CV^2,\qquad C:=\frac{2\pi\varepsilon}{\ln(b/a)};$$ the instantaneous per-length energies are $\tfrac12CV^2\cos^2\theta$ and $\tfrac12LI^2\cos^2\theta$ with $\theta=kx_3-\omega t$; equivalently, with $L:=\mu\ln(b/a)/(2\pi)$ and the boundary-current amplitude $I:=2\pi V/(Z\ln(b/a))$ one has $W_m=\tfrac12LI^2$ and $LC=\varepsilon\mu$. The two boundary components carrying distinct constants are exactly what the single-conductor obstruction excludes.
(d) [Scope] The obstruction clause (b) is proved for the continuous-boundary harmonic-potential form. The star-shaped interior classification in (a) covers both signs and the zero field, with boundary conclusions under the stated potential-trace hypotheses; the general reduction of an arbitrary TEM field to the potential form on a merely simply connected non-star-shaped cross-section is not asserted here. The coaxial clause is an explicit conditional computation in the declared model with no empirical content; no lossy, radiation or signal-speed claim is made.
after.strategy:
For (a), each real and imaginary plane harmonic potential component is smooth in the interior by [[thm-plane-harmonic-functions-are-smooth-and-real-analytic]]. Hence the constructed fields and their constant-coefficient polarization/magnetization representatives have the interior regularity required by the smooth macroscopic supplier; the stated boundary potential trace is used separately for PEC. Work componentwise with the complex potential: $	ilde E=-
abla\varphi$ is closed and divergence-free because $\Delta\varphi=0$. With $	ilde H= eta e_z	imes	ilde E/(\omega\mu)$ and $ eta^2=\varepsilon\mu\omega^2$, [[lem-em-separated-phasor-calculus]] and [[lem-em-transverse-vector-identities]] (applied separately to real and imaginary parts) verify the two curl equations and both divergences. Conversely a $C^1$ TEM amplitude has $E_z=H_z=0$. The longitudinal components of the curl equations give $\operatorname{curl}_2	ilde E=\operatorname{curl}_2	ilde H=0$, and Gauss gives both transverse divergences zero. The transverse Faraday equation is $i eta e_z	imes	ilde E=i\omega\mu	ilde H$, so $	ilde H= eta e_z	imes	ilde E/(\omega\mu)$ without division by $ eta$. Substituting into Ampere yields $( eta^2-\varepsilon\mu\omega^2)	ilde E=0$. If $	ilde E
e0$, this gives both roots $ eta=\pm\omega/v$; if $	ilde E=0$, Faraday forces $	ilde H=0$ and the label $ eta$ is unrestricted. On a star-shaped domain the closed-field supplier gives real potentials for the real and imaginary parts, hence a complex $C^2$ interior potential with $	ilde E=-
abla\varphi$ after a sign change; Gauss makes it harmonic. No real-only or boundary-extension conclusion is inferred from interior exactness. If the potential has the stated differentiable trace, $	au=e_z	imes n$ gives $n\cdot(e_z	imes	ilde E)=\partial_	au\varphi$ and $n	imes	ilde E=-e_z\partial_	au\varphi$. Thus PEC is equivalent to the zero tangential derivative. The chain rule and FTC [[thm-ftc-second-part]] on boundary charts make the trace locally constant, and connectedness makes it constant on each boundary component. For (b), apply [[cor-uniqueness-for-the-classical-dirichlet-problem]] to the real and imaginary potential components and their constant boundary values; it requires only bounded nonempty open $A$, not a smooth boundary, and hence also covers the rectangle under the stated trace. For the rectangular class with continuous-closure amplitudes, the explicit radial primitive from an interior star centre is an integral of the continuous amplitude along segments of the closed rectangle, so it extends continuously to the closure. On an open edge, pass the interior line-integral FTC identity to the edge using uniform continuity of the amplitude; its trace has tangential derivative minus the tangential electric amplitude. PEC makes this zero, and the connected edges have equal constants by continuity at corners. The uniqueness supplier then applies to each harmonic component without a false smooth-boundary assumption. For (c), keep the forward real-potential example exactly as displayed with $k=\omega/v$: direct logarithmic differentiation and the chain rule give $\Delta\varphi=0$, and the radial/tangential amplitudes satisfy both curl equations and PEC on the two circles. Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the polar Lebesgue formula [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]] applies to the continuous nonnegative squared amplitudes on the annulus. Its angular normalization in dimension2 is $2\pi$: equivalently use the $C^1$ polar diffeomorphism $(r,	heta)\mapsto(r\cos	heta,r\sin	heta)$ on $(a,b)	imes(0,2\pi)$, with Jacobian $r$, using [[cor-c-one-change-of-variables-for-l-one-functions]]. The omitted radial segment is Lebesgue null by [[prop-degenerate-boxes-and-coordinate-hyperplanes-are-lebesgue-null]]. The finite radial integral is $\int_a^b dr/r=\log(b/a)$ by [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]], so $\int_A|	ilde E|^2=\int_A|Z	ilde H|^2=2\pi V^2/\log(b/a)$. Substitution gives all displayed capacitance, inductance and energy formulas and $LC=\varepsilon\mu$; the zero value $V=0$ gives zero fields and energies. Only the local smooth energy-reading clause is used. Construction, the two-sign/zero classification and the potential-form obstruction are choice-free; Countable Choice is confined to the explicitly stated polar-measure energy branch, with no empirical premise.
after.physical_scope: The explicit coaxial TEM candidate of the lossless isotropic scalar branch with its per-length capacitance and inductance, and the obstruction showing that a single-conductor cross-section with connected boundary admits no nonzero TEM field in the harmonic-potential form. Includes complex potentials, both propagation signs, the zero-field label case and the star-shaped interior reduction with explicit boundary traces; no general simply connected reduction, lossy or empirical claim.

before.title: Rectangular PEC reflection class: Fourier completeness, weak solutions and energy conservation
before.statement: Let $Q=\prod_{j=1}^3(0,L_j)$ with $L_j>0$ and let $\varepsilon,\mu>0$ be constants. Define the reflection boundary class by extending $E_1$ evenly across the $x_1$-walls and oddly across the $x_2,x_3$-walls, and cyclically for $E_2,E_3$; extend $B_1$ oddly across $x_1$ and evenly across $x_2,x_3$, cyclically for $B_2,B_3$. Work on the rectangular torus $\prod_j\mathbb R/(2L_j\mathbb Z)$ in the real $L^2$ fields with these parities and distributional $\operatorname{div}E=\operatorname{div}B=0$. For smooth fields the parity class gives $n\times E=0$ and $n\cdot B=0$ on $\partial Q$. Then: (i) the finite separated Fourier modes are dense in this class, and the class is complete for the $L^2$ pairing ([[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]], [[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]); (ii) for every initial datum in the class there is a unique $C(\mathbb R;L^2)$ weak solution of $\partial_tE=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1}\operatorname{curl}B$, $\partial_tB=-\operatorname{curl}E$ in the same class ([[def-distributional-derivative]]); (iii) the energy $\tfrac12\int_Q(\varepsilon|E|^2+|B|^2/\mu)\,dx$ is constant along the solution. This is an explicit weak PEC model; it supplies neither trace regularity for arbitrary $H(\operatorname{curl})$ fields nor completeness in lossy, open or non-rectangular guides.
before.strategy: The one-dimensional character system on the torus is complete for complex $L^2$ ([[thm-trigonometric-system-is-complete-in-l-two-of-the-torus]]) and its Fourier partial sums converge in mean square ([[thm-l-two-fourier-series-converges-in-mean-square]]). If an $L^2(Q)$ function is orthogonal to every product of characters, fix two indices and integrate against those two characters: Fubini and Cauchy-Schwarz ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]) make the remaining one-variable coefficient an $L^2$ function whose character coefficients all vanish, hence it is zero; repeating in the second and third coordinates on a single null set gives product completeness; orthogonality follows by iterated one-variable integration and Parseval by expanding the squared distance to a finite projection. Reflection parities force sine in odd coordinates and cosine in even coordinates; the trigonometric product modes are the paired $\pm k_j$ projections. For each torus wavevector $k_j=\pi n_j/L_j$ the Fourier coefficients satisfy the finite-dimensional constant-coefficient linear system $\widehat E_t=i(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1}k\times\widehat B$, $\widehat B_t=-ik\times\widehat E$ with $k\cdot\widehat E=k\cdot\widehat B=0$. The system is Lipschitz, so the maximal-solution theorem ([[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]]) gives a unique solution through the initial coefficients, and differentiating $\varepsilon|\widehat E|^2+|\widehat B|^2/\mu$ gives zero by the scalar triple-product identity and conjugation, so its weighted norm is preserved and the solution is global; the constrained subspace and the parity patterns are preserved because $k\cdot(k\times v)=0$ and curl maps the stated parities into each other. Solve all coefficients, truncate to finitely many wavevectors, and pass to the limit with Parseval: the weighted tail norm equals its initial value, so the finite solutions converge uniformly in time in $L^2$, and the limit is $C_tL^2$ and satisfies the equations in the distributional sense ([[def-distributional-derivative]]) after testing against smooth periodic compactly supported-in-time tests, whose coefficients and derivatives are summable. Uniqueness: a $C_tL^2$ weak solution has continuous Fourier coefficients whose distributional derivatives are the displayed continuous right-hand sides; testing the difference of two solutions against smooth periodic tests and using the vanishing of the difference's distributional derivative yields equality of the coefficients, and energy conservation passes to the limit in norm.

Identify the complex coefficient space with its finite-dimensional real and imaginary parts. The constant linear right-hand side is globally state-Lipschitz on all time and state space, so [[cor-globally-lipschitz-odes-have-global-solutions]] gives a unique global solution through the initial coefficients. Differentiating $\varepsilon|\widehat E|^2+|\widehat B|^2/\mu$ gives zero by the scalar triple-product identity and conjugation, so its weighted norm is preserved; the constrained subspace and the parity patterns are preserved because $k\cdot(k\times v)=0$ and curl maps the stated parities into each other. No absolute summability of test Fourier coefficients is needed. Uniqueness: a $C_tL^2$ weak solution has continuous Fourier coefficients whose distributional derivatives are the displayed continuous right-hand sides; for each coefficient $z(t)$ and its continuous right-hand side $g(t)$, subtract the classical primitive $G(t)=\int_0^t g(s)\,ds$. FTC gives $G'=g$, so $z-G$ has zero distributional derivative. [[thm-a-distribution-with-zero-derivatives-on-a-connected-open-set-is-constant]] on $\mathbb R$ makes this regular distribution constant; continuity makes the equality pointwise. Thus each coefficient is a classical solution of the displayed finite-dimensional ODE, and global ODE uniqueness with its given initial value identifies it. Product completeness then identifies the fields. Energy conservation passes to the limit in norm. Countable Choice covers the Fourier, Fubini, Hilbert-space and regular-distribution supplier contracts; the finite-dimensional modal equations require no extra choice premise.

before.title: Spectral completeness of the curl operator in a smooth PEC cavity
before.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice, as used by the complete variational, Sobolev-extension and compact-spectral suppliers. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded $C^\infty$ domain. Define $H(\operatorname{curl})=\{u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):\operatorname{curl}u\in L^2\}$ and $H(\operatorname{div})=\{u\in L^2:\operatorname{div}u\in L^2\}$ with their graph norms, and let $X$ be the graph-norm closure in $H(\operatorname{curl})\cap H(\operatorname{div})$ of the smooth fields on the closure with $n\times u=0$; this is an explicit weak perfect-electric-conductor boundary class. Put $V=\{u\in X:\operatorname{div}u=0\}$ and $H=\overline{V}^{\,L^2}$. Then the curl form on $V$ has a complete orthonormal $L^2$ eigenbasis with nonnegative eigenvalues $\lambda_j$ of finite multiplicity tending to infinity whenever $H$ is infinite dimensional, and the zero eigenspace is finite dimensional and must be retained when the topology allows it. Each eigenfield $u_j\in V$ satisfies the full graph-class variational identity $\int_\Omega\operatorname{curl}u_j\cdot\operatorname{curl}v=\lambda_j\int_\Omega u_j\cdot v$ for every $v\in X$. after.title: Spectral completeness of the curl operator in a smooth PEC cavity
after.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice, as used by the complete variational, Sobolev-extension and compact-spectral suppliers. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded $C^\infty$ domain. Put $V=\{u\in X:\operatorname{div}u=0\}$ and $H=\overline{V}^{\,L^2}$. Then the curl form on $V$ has a complete orthonormal $L^2$ eigenbasis with nonnegative eigenvalues $\lambda_j$ of finite multiplicity tending to infinity whenever $H$ is infinite dimensional, and the zero eigenspace is finite dimensional and must be retained when the topology allows it. The eigen equation is $$\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}u_j=\lambda_ju_j$$ distributionally with the PEC trace, and for every explicitly chosen mathematical speed $v_{\mathrm{wave}}>0$ and every initial displacement $q_0\in V$ and velocity $q_1\in H$, the associated second-order wave has coefficients $a_j''+v_{\mathrm{wave}}^2\lambda_ja_j=0$ with those initial coefficients. Its displacement lies in $C(\mathbb R;V)$ and its velocity in $C(\mathbb R;H)$; finite modal sums converge respectively in $C(K;V)$ and $C(K;H)$ on every compact time interval $K$. The finite-dimensional $\lambda=0$ sector is retained with $a_j(t)=a_j(0)+ta_j'(0)$. This speed is a positive abstract mathematical parameter, not a physical constant or prerequisite. No identification with every maximal tangential-trace realisation, and no lossy, open or non-smooth-domain spectral claim, is made.

before.title: Spectral completeness of the declared PEC waveguide and cavity classes
before.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the explicitly used variational, Sobolev and compact-spectral suppliers. Let the PEC classes be those of [[lem-em-smooth-pec-cavity-spectral-closure]]: for a bounded $C^\infty$ domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$, $X$ is the graph-norm closure in $H(\operatorname{curl})\cap H(\operatorname{div})$ of the smooth fields on the closure with $n\times u=0$, $V=\{u\in X:\operatorname{div}u=0\}$ and $H=\overline V^{\,L^2}$. Then:
(a) **Smooth cavity.** The curl form on $V$ has a complete orthonormal $L^2$ eigenbasis $\{u_j\}$ with nonnegative eigenvalues $\lambda_j$ of finite multiplicity, $\lambda_j\to\infty$ whenever $H$ is infinite dimensional, and a finite-dimensional zero eigenspace that is retained; the eigen-equation $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}u_j=\lambda_ju_j$ holds distributionally with the PEC trace. The eigenfields are $C^\infty$ on the closure by [[lem-em-pec-cavity-eigenfield-boundary-regularity]], applied to the full-$X$ eigenvariational identity of the cavity supplier. The shifted scalar auxiliary boundary problems are solvable on the declared bounded smooth domain by [[thm-em-elliptic-boundary-existence]]; the specific scalar Dirichlet resolvent and its smooth-zero-boundary test density used in G3 are supplied by its recorded local resolvent lemma.
(b) **Rectangular class.** For a rectangular box the separable products described in the mode verification are dense in the reflection-parity energy class, and every initial datum of that class has a unique $C(\mathbb R;L^2)$ weak solution of $\partial_tE=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1}\operatorname{curl}B$, $\partial_tB=-\operatorname{curl}E$ in the class with constant energy, with finite separated modes dense at every time. The rectangular statements are the recorded rectangular reflection-class completeness lemma [[lem-em-rectangular-pec-energy-completeness]] (the $G2$ branch); the individual TE/TM mode verification against the Maxwell equations and the PEC conditions is the recorded $G1$ physics branch, homed on the physical guide page and not consumed here as a mathematical premise. No completeness in lossy, open-ended or non-smooth classes is asserted.
before.strategy: The smooth-cavity spectral and finite-energy assertions are exactly [[lem-em-smooth-pec-cavity-spectral-closure]]: its shifted coercive full-$X$ solution operator, divergence projection using the proved scalar Dirichlet resolvent and smooth-zero-boundary density, and compact self-adjoint spectral theorem give the complete $H^1$ graph-class eigenbasis, multiplicities, distributional equations and modal wave expansion with topology zero modes retained. ## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable choice, open sets $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$, a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $T : U \to V$, and a function $f \in L^1(\lambda_n)$.

[L1] Compact-support Riemann substitution holds. Continuous functions on boxes are Riemann integrable, equivalently their Darboux sums converge. Box Lebesgue measure equals volume and coordinate faces are null under countable choice. ([[cor-change-of-variables-for-compactly-supported-functions]], [[thm-continuous-on-a-rectangle-is-riemann-integrable]], [[thm-multidimensional-darboux-equals-riemann]], [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]], [[prop-degenerate-boxes-and-coordinate-hyperplanes-are-lebesgue-null]])

[L5] Rational boxes generate Euclidean Borel sets; Dynkin's theorem extends equality of finite measures from a generating pi-system. A nonnegative density defines a measure. ([[thm-rational-box-generators-of-the-borel-sigma-algebra-on-rn]], [[thm-dynkin-pi-lambda]], [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]])

[L2] Lebesgue measurable sets differ from Borel sets only inside Borel null sets, under countable choice. ([[cor-lebesgue-sigma-algebra-is-the-completion-of-borel-lebesgue-measure]], [[def-countable-choice]])

[L3] A nonnegative measurable function has zero integral exactly when it vanishes almost everywhere; integrals on measurable null sets vanish. ([[thm-nonnegative-integral-zero-iff-zero-almost-everywhere]], [[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]])

[L4] Nonnegative integrals are additive and obey monotone convergence; complex integrals are linear on $L^1$. ([[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]], [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]], [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]])

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 First identify continuous compact-support Riemann and Lebesgue integrals locally. Extend a continuous compactly supported function on an open set by zero; this is continuous because its support is compact inside that open set. On a bounding closed box it is bounded and Riemann integrable by [L1]. Its lower and upper grid step functions, disjointifying cells along null coordinate faces, have Lebesgue integrals equal to the lower and upper Darboux sums. Their difference tends to zero. After adding a fixed constant to make all functions nonnegative, monotonicity squeezes the Lebesgue integral to the Riemann integral; subtract the constant using finite integrability. Apply this to $k\in C_c(V)$ and $(k\circ T)|\det DT|$, whose support is contained in the compact preimage of $\operatorname{supp}k$. Riemann substitution [L1] therefore proves the Lebesgue substitution formula for $k$. [L1, L4, given]

2.1 For Borel $E\subseteq V$, let $\alpha(E)=\lambda_n(E)$ and $\beta(E)=\int_{T^{-1}(E)}J\,dx$, with $J=|\det DT|$. These are Borel measures by [L5]. For an open rational box $R$ with compact closure in $V$, the continuous functions $k_j(y)=\min(1,j\operatorname{dist}(y,\mathbb R^n\setminus R))$ have support in $\overline R$ and increase to $1_R$. Step 1.1 and monotone convergence give $\alpha(R)=\beta(R)<\infty$. List all such boxes as $(R_j)$ and set $W_j=\bigcup_{i\le j}R_i$. They exhaust $V$; finite inclusion-exclusion, whose terms are finite and are boxes or empty, gives agreement on $W_j$ and $W_j\cap R$ for every such box $R$. Thus the finite measures $E\mapsto\alpha(E\cap W_j)$ and $E\mapsto\beta(E\cap W_j)$ agree on the pi-system of these boxes, the empty set and $V$. This pi-system generates the Borel sets because the boxes form a countable basis of $V$. The equality class is a lambda-system: equal finite total masses allow complements and countable additivity allows disjoint unions. Apply [L5], then take $j\to\infty$, to obtain $\alpha=\beta$ on all Borel sets. If $V$ is empty there is nothing to prove. [L4, L5, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 The Borel set equality of step 2.1 gives substitution for nonnegative Borel simple functions by finite sums. Explicit increasing dyadic simple approximations and [L4] extend it to all nonnegative Borel functions. This establishes the Borel formula locally without a later-page supplier. [L4, step 2.1]

4.1 Put $J=|\det DT|$, continuous and strictly positive since $T$ is a diffeomorphism. If $Z\subseteq V$ is Borel null, step 3.1 gives $\int_U1_Z(T(x))J(x)\,dx=0$. By [L3] and positivity of $J$, the Borel set $T^{-1}(Z)$ is null. Countable choice is used in the Borel construction and the completion interface [L2], not in the finite real/imaginary decomposition below. [L1, L2, L3, given]

5.1 For Lebesgue measurable $E\subseteq V$, write $E=A\cup N$ with $A$ Borel and $N\subseteq Z$ for Borel null $Z$, intersecting all sets with $V$. Then $T^{-1}(E)$ is a Borel set modified inside the Borel null set $T^{-1}(Z)$, hence measurable by [L2]. The indicator functions of $E,A$ and their pullbacks agree off the respective null sets, so [L3] and step 3.1 give $\lambda_n(E)=\int_U1_E(T(x))J(x)\,dx$. [L1, L2, L3, step 4.1]

6.1 Finite nonnegative sums give substitution for nonnegative simple Lebesgue measurable functions. For any nonnegative measurable $h$, the explicit simple functions $s_k=2^{-k}\lfloor2^k\min(h,k)\rfloor$ increase to $h$. Step 5.1 ensures measurability of their pullbacks, hence of $h\circ T$. By [L4], passing to the increasing limits proves $\int_Vh=\int_U(h\circ T)J$. [L4, step 5.1, construct]

7.1 Apply step 6.1 first to $|f|$. It gives $\int_U|f\circ T|J=\int_V|f|<\infty$, so the transformed complex function is integrable. Write $f=u-v+i(p-q)$ using the nonnegative positive and negative parts of its real and imaginary parts; each is bounded by $|f|$. Apply step 6.1 to these four functions and recombine their finite integrals by [L4]. This proves the stated identity. [L4, step 6.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Functions $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$.

[L1] Holder's inequality holds for conjugate exponents ([[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]]).

[L2] The strict-exponent equality criterion for Holder has already been proved ([[thm-equality-case-in-holder-inequality]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** Specialize Holder to $p=q=2$, and inherit the equality clause from the strict-exponent equality theorem.

1.1 The exponent $2$ is conjugate to itself, so [L1] with $p=q=2$ gives [L1] $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$ [L1]

2.1 Because $2>1$, the equality clause is exactly the specialization of [L2] to [L2, step 1.1] $p=q=2$. [L2, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and star-shaped, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$. The following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is closed;
2. $F$ is exact;
3. $F$ is conservative;
4. $F$ is path-independent;
5. every closed piecewise-$C^1$ path $\gamma$ in $U$ satisfies $\int_\gamma F\cdot d\mathbf r=0$.

## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The star-shaped domain and $C^1$ field in the Statement.

[L1] A star-shaped open set is nonempty and contains every segment from a star centre to a point of the set ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]).

[L2] Exactness uses a $C^2$ potential, whereas conservativity uses a $C^1$ potential ([[def-closed-and-exact-c1-vector-fields]], [[def-piecewise-c1-path-connected-conservative-and-path-independent]]).

[L3] Every exact $C^1$ field is closed, and every closed $C^1$ field on a star-shaped domain is exact ([[thm-exact-c1-vector-fields-are-closed]], [[thm-poincare-lemma-for-star-shaped-domains]]).

[L4] For a continuous field on a nonempty open piecewise-$C^1$ path-connected domain, conservativity, path independence, and the zero-loop condition are equivalent ([[thm-conservative-path-independent-and-zero-loop-equivalence]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 If $a$ is a star centre, any $x,y\in U$ are joined by the segment from $x$ to $a$ followed by the segment from $a$ to $y$. By [L1] these segments lie in $U$, so $U$ is piecewise-$C^1$ path-connected. [given, L1]

1.2 Conditions 1 and 2 are equivalent by the two implications in [L3]. [given, L3]

1.3 Condition 2 implies condition 3 by [L2]. Conversely, if $F=\nabla\phi$ with $\phi$ merely $C^1$, then the first partials of $\phi$ are the components of the $C^1$ field $F$; hence $\phi$ is $C^2$, and condition 2 holds. [given, L2, algebra]

2.1 By step 1.1, all hypotheses of [L4] hold, so conditions 3, 4, and 5 are equivalent. [step 1.1, L4]

3.1 Combining steps 1.2, 1.3, and 2.1 proves the five-way equivalence. [step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Reals $x,y$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Apply the addition law to $x+iy$ and Euler's formula. [given]

1.2 Multiplicativity of modulus, the Pythagorean identity, and positivity of $e^x$ give the modulus formula. [given]

2.1 The defining quarter-turn value $\cos\pi=-1$ and $\sin\pi=0$ give Euler's identity. [given] ∎

## Statement

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a bounded $C^1$ domain or have the specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation. For real $u\in C^2(\overline\Omega)$ and $v\in C^1(\overline\Omega)$, $$\int_\Omega(v\Delta u+Du\cdot Dv)\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}v\partial_\nu u\,dS.$$ In the piecewise case the right side is the sum over faces, counted once off E. All integrals are finite.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, a bounded C1 domain or the specified finite piecewise C1 class in dimension $n\ge2$, and real $u\in C^2(\overline\Omega)$, $v\in C^1(\overline\Omega)$.

[F1] The divergence formula holds for a C1 field up to a C1 boundary. ([[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-c-one-euclidean-domains]]).

[F2] The divergence formula holds for the specified finite faces. ([[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-piecewise-c-one-domains]]).

[F3] The normal derivative is the gradient dotted with the outward normal. ([[def-classical-normal-derivative]]).

[F4] The product rule applies to scalar derivatives. ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]).

## Proof

1.1 Set $F_i=v\partial_i u$. On each coordinate line inside Omega the product rule F4 gives $\partial_iF_i=(\partial_i v)(\partial_i u)+v\partial_i^2u$; the same rule for every $\partial_jF_i$ shows that F and all its first derivatives extend continuously to the closure. Thus $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$ and summing over i gives $\operatorname{div}F=Du\cdot Dv+v\Delta u$. [given, F4, algebra]

2.1 On every regular boundary point F3 gives $F\cdot\nu=v(Du\cdot\nu)=v\partial_\nu u$. Apply F1 in the C1 case and F2 in the specified piecewise case to the field from step 1.1. Substituting its divergence and flux gives exactly the displayed identity. Continuous derivatives and functions on the compact closure are bounded; finite volume and the finite surface measures in F1/F2 prove absolute integrability. The edge set contributes zero to each face integral. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $F:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and suppose one $L\ge0$ satisfies $\|F(t,x)-F(t,y)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2$ for all $t,x,y$. Then every IVP for $x'=F(t,x)$ has a unique global solution.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The globally state-Lipschitz field and its maximal solution.

[L1] Gronwall bounds a nonnegative function by its forcing and a linear integral term ([[thm-gronwall-integral-inequality]]).

[L2] At a finite maximal endpoint the solution leaves every compact subset of the ODE domain ([[cor-finite-maximal-time-forces-escape-from-every-compact-set]]).

[L3] A continuous real-valued function on a nonempty compact metric space is bounded ([[thm-extreme-value-metric]]).

[L4] A solution satisfies its associated Volterra integral equation ([[prop-first-order-ivp-is-equivalent-to-a-volterra-integral-equation]]).

[L5] Closed bounded subsets of $\mathbb R^n$ are compact ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

[L6] Every Picard–Lindelöf IVP has a unique maximal solution, and every other solution through the same data is its restriction ([[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** contradiction.

1.1 Let $x$ be the unique maximal solution supplied by [L6], and suppose, for contradiction, that one of its maximal endpoints is finite. On a finite time slab reaching toward it, [L3] bounds $\|F(t,0)\|_2$ by $M$ and global Lipschitz continuity gives $\|F(t,x)\|_2\le M+L\|x\|_2$; [L4] and [L1] therefore bound $\|x(t)\|_2$ throughout the slab. [given, L1, L3, L4, L6, assume-contra]

2.1 By [L5], step 1.1 places the graph near that endpoint in a compact time-state box, contradicting [L2]; hence both endpoints are infinite and the solution is global. [step 1.1, L2, L5, discharge-contradiction] ∎

## Statement

Let $n\ge2$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be bounded, nonempty and open. Two functions $u,v\in C^2(\Omega)\cap C(\overline\Omega)$ with $\Delta u=\Delta v$ in $\Omega$ and $u=v$ on $\partial\Omega$ agree on $\overline\Omega$. Thus prescribed classical Poisson equation and Dirichlet data have at most one such solution. Moreover, for equal Laplacians,
$$\sup_{\overline\Omega}|u-v|\le\sup_{\partial\Omega}|u-v|.$$
In particular, a sequence of such solutions with a common Laplacian and uniformly convergent boundary traces converges uniformly on the closure.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The objects and hypotheses in the statement.

[F1] On a bounded nonempty open set, $\Delta u\ge\Delta v$ and boundary $u\le v$ imply closure $u\le v$ for $C^2$ interior, continuous-closure functions. ([[thm-comparison-principle-for-classical-subharmonic-functions]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Comparison applied to $(u,v)$ and then $(v,u)$ gives $u\le v$ and $v\le u$, respectively, proving uniqueness. [F1, given]

1.2 For possibly different boundary values put $b=\max_{\partial\Omega}|u-v|$. It is finite because the boundary is nonempty compact and the difference is continuous. Compare $u$ with $v+b$ and $v$ with $u+b$; their Laplacians agree. Hence $|u-v|\le b$ on the closure. [F1, algebra]

2.1 For a sequence with common Laplacian, the bound just proved applies to every pair of terms. Uniformly convergent boundary traces are uniformly Cauchy, so the solutions are uniformly Cauchy on the closure. Completeness of the real numbers supplies the pointwise limit and the same Cauchy bound makes convergence uniform. The limit is continuous there, as follows by combining a uniform error bound with continuity of a fixed term. [step 1.2, algebra] ∎
